https://www.dw.com/en/jews-once-lived-li.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MaOj A 1930 photograph of Salomo Birnbaum (standing) and his family, who had to leave their home in Germany and flee to London Image: David Birnbaum/Nathan & Solomon Birnbaum Archives, Toronto Advertisement Over the years, many people have passed through this fourth-floor apartment in an old Berlin building. Here, at Rosenheimer Straße 40, they have sat on the sofa and gathered around the kitchen table. They have looked out the window and let their minds wander. Marie Rolshoven has lived here with her family since 2007. "The feeling of crossing that threshold, the same one the former residents crossed for the last time, stays with you," she says. She knows that Jews once lived here, and none of them survived the Nazi era. Driven from their homes After the National Socialists seized power in January 1933, it quickly became clear that Jews were considered second-class citizens under Nazi rule. Even the right to remain in their homes could no longer be taken for granted. "A racially conscious fellow citizen cannot be expected to share a household with a Jew," the Nazi party newspaper Völkischer Beobachter wrote on September 18, 1938, claiming that landlords were therefore entitled to terminate leases without notice. On April 30, 1939, the law took effect. Jewish tenants and property owners were forced to leave their homes and move into buildings designated by the authorities, referred to in Nazi jargon as "Judenhäuser"(Jewish houses). Several people were forcibly housed in Henny and Carl Möller's apartment at Rosenheimer Straße 40. In the end, there were nine of them. In the fall of 1941, Nazi authorities began systematically deporting Jews to ghettos and camps in Eastern Europe. Jews were deported not only from Germany, but from throughout Europe Image: Scherl/SZ Photo/picture alliance Propaganda Minister Joseph Goebbels wrote in his diary: "The main thing is that the capital of the Reich be cleansed of Jews; and I will neither rest nor relent until this goal is fully achieved." The residents of Rosenheimer Straße were among those who were subsequently deported. Remembering at the original site Marie Rolshoven aims to honor the fate of these individuals. In 2016, she, along with her late mother and a friend, founded the initiative Denk Mal Am Ort (a wordplay meaning both "Think about it at the site" and "Memorial at the Site") inspired by the Amsterdam project Open Jewish Homes. Marie Rolshoven (left) hosted the niece of a Jewish woman (right) who once lived in her apartment and was murdered by the Nazis Image: KUBIN e.V. The idea is to invite people to the very location where everyday life once occurred. "You feel a strong connection to these individuals through the actual site," says Rolshoven. "It's different from visiting a memorial." 'My brother's bed used to be right here' Two floors below, her neighbors had a similar experience. Denk Mal Am Ort found out that the Jewish Katzenellenbogen family had previously rented the apartment. The family escaped Nazi Germany in 1939, just in time. "In 2018, 92-year-old Joel Ludwig Katzenellenbogen was invited back here, accompanied by his daughter, son-in-law, and grandson,” Rolshoven tells DW. The Denk Mal Am Ort initiative discovered him through Facebook. Rolshoven recounts how touched the visitors were when the former resident walked in and remarked, "Yes, I remember it clearly. My brother's bed used to be right here. He was 10 when we had to leave the country." In 2018, Joel Ludwig Katzenellenbogen (seated middle) visited the apartment where he'd spent his childhood Image: KUBIN e.V. Soon there will be no eyewitnesses left Joel Ludwig Katzenellenbogen has since passed away, along with many other eyewitnesses. This highlights the importance of intergenerational remembrance, according to Rolshoven. She has already welcomed a descendant of a former resident into her home. Claudia Samter's mother managed to escape from Berlin to Argentina, but her aunt was not as fortunate. Seeking assistance in tracing her family's history, Claudia contacted Denk Mal Am Ort. It turned out that her aunt had once been housed in Rolshoven's apartment. Claudia Samter has already visited twice. "After all, there's no grave in a cemetery for her to visit," says Rolshoven. "We sat at the kitchen table to talk about life today and tomorrow, and we laughed a lot and cried, too. It felt good to give this space a new purpose once again." Claudia Samter (standing right) tells 'Denk Mal Am Ort' visitors about her murdered aunt, who once lived in this apartment Image: KUBIN e.V. Denk Mal Am Ort has so far organized 90 commemorative events in eight cities this year. Many young descendants attended, according to Rolshoven. "Knowing that they had stood in this stairwell and touched the same doorknob helped them." Seeking traces of ancestors 19-year-old Adam Ethan Klein from Switzerland also wanted to learn more about his ancestors' history. "I always knew there was a story of escape, but it was never a significant topic at home,” he says. "They'd say, ‘Yes, your great-grandparents left Germany in 1938, just in time. Luckily, otherwise you wouldn't be here today'." Klein says his decision to dig deeper was prompted by the spread of antisemitism , as well as the widespread slogan "Never again is now." (Editor's note: This slogan serves as a call to actively confront antisemitism, hatred, and threats to democracy today.) The whole family was aware of a suitcase belonging to his maternal great-grandfather in the attic. However, no one ever looked inside until Adam finally opened the suitcase and discovered dozens of documents. He also found a letter from the Hanover District Court dated June 12, 1933, addressed to his great-grandfather, attorney Max Haas. This suitcase in his grandmother's attic piqued Adam's curiosity Image: privat The letter stated: "As of today, following the decree issued by the Minister of Justice, you have been removed from the list of licensed attorneys." 'They were above all one thing: Jews' Klein was profoundly affected by the letter: "With this single sentence, it became unmistakably clear to the families that they were not quite what they had aspired to be for generations: an average German family. From that moment on, they were above all one thing: Jews." For Klein, this was a troubling realization. So was the news that someone had stabbed an ultra-Orthodox Jew to death in Zurich while shouting antisemitic slogans. The attack occurred not far from the synagogue where he had shortly before celebrated a cousin's bar mitzvah. (Editor's note: In Judaism, a bar mitzvah is a ceremony that marks a young person's coming of age in religious matters.) "For the first time in my life, I felt that unsettling sensation of not quite belonging. Yet Zurich is my home, the city where I've lived carefree as a Jewish Swiss from birth," Adam would later write. "That was definitely new, uncharted territory for me. I had always thought that such things don't happen in Switzerland. Maybe that was a bit naive of me," he admits. The subject would not let him go. Adam continued his research, determined to write his high school graduation thesis about his relatives. In the spring of 2024, he set off with his parents, sister, grandmother, uncles, aunts and several cousins to visit the places where their ancestors had lived. A magical encounter At some point during their journey, they found themselves in Stuttgart, standing in front of a five-story building at Hölderlinstraße 55, when a man on a bike emerged from the courtyard and approached them. "So, are you taking a guided tour of the city, or are you planning to move here?" he asked jokingly. The man was Thomas Koch, who had spent time researching the former residents of his house. When he heard the answer, "No, we're just checking out where our ancestors lived," he was thrilled. Adam Ethan Klein (right, light pants, blue sweater) and his relatives meet Thomas Koch (center, in reflector vest) Image: privat Koch had already discovered that the former owners of the house, the Merzbacher brothers, sold it in 1936 for 75,000 Reichsmarks. From that amount, they had to pay 70,000 Reichsmarks in wealth taxes and the Reich Emigration Tax. The remaining sum was just enough to cover the ship fares to Brazil and the United States. From 1937 to 1938, a family named Hirschheimer, who worked in the plywood trade, lived on the ground floor before they were forcibly relocated to a "Judenhaus." Their trail went cold in 1939, as Koch found no further records. So, he asked, "Are you the Hirschheimer family?" They were indeed. Koch describes the encounter as magical. Adolf and Auguste Hirschheimer were Adam's great-great-grandparents, and their daughter, Ilse, was married to Max Haas. Adam Klein and Thomas Koch have kept in touch since then. The next time Adam visited Stuttgart, he was invited over for coffee and cake. Adolf and Auguste Hirschheimer lived with their daughter Ilse in the place where Thomas Koch now lives Image: privat Adam was impressed by the beautiful apartment. "It was fascinating to imagine how my ancestors once lived there, and it probably wasn't that different. Back then, there was likely coffee and cake as well." Adam showed Koch photos of his grandmother, Ilse, who had married at the synagogue in Stuttgart, standing in the living room in her wedding gown. "In front of the door that we still have," says Koch. “It was really moving to discover new roommates in a historical context set in the past. And I think this experience — this process of putting myself in their shoes — is a deeply empathetic one that simply brings us together through this apartment.” Shattered identities Ilse and Max Haas found refuge in England, while the Hirschheimers emigrated to Switzerland in 1939. Adolf Hirschheimer died in 1940 from a heart condition, but Adam, his great-great-grandson, believes he "certainly also died of a broken heart." Thomas Koch (right) and Adam Ethan Klein have presented their joint investigation to audiences on several occasions Image: privat Auguste was brought to England by her son-in-law, Max, where the family felt homesick. "There, we were the Jews; here, we are the Germans. Try figuring that out," Ilse Haas wrote to a friend. Adam chose these lines as the title for his thesis. Adam's great-grandparents could not find peace after being stripped of their homeland. From England, they eventually went to Israel and, at some point, returned to Europe — to Switzerland. "At the end of their lives, my great-grandparents settled just a two-hour drive from their old homeland," Adam wrote. "When I look at their lives through the eyes of a great-grandson, it becomes clear that after breaking ties with Germany, they never managed to put down roots anywhere again." "Remembering is important because, ultimately, we have to learn from history," says Adam. "And I think every single person has a responsibility— and the power — to actively keep memories alive. And hopefully, that can happen even without eyewitnesses.” For example, in his ancestors' former apartment. This article was originally written in German. In Germany, France, Belgium and the Netherlands, a combined shortage of 3,1 million tons compared to the five-year average harvest is expected. The data shows the weak harvest will hit Germany particularly hard, with the country's share of the total expected potato harvest shortage coming in at 1,13 million tons. These figures do not yet represent a final harvest report, but are an estimate. "As fall begins, the effects of the record-breaking summer heat and drought on food and agriculture are becoming clear," said ECIU analyst Tom Lancaster. Potatoes are among the crops in Europe that require the most water. The analysis also reports a significant increase in prices. In Germany, spuds served at dinner are set to cost up to €280 per metric ton, compared to around €150 last year. "Any system will have to comply with data protection rules and minimize the amount of information that is collected about the user, without age-verification data being transmitted online. However, the primary responsibility for protecting minors lies with the social media platforms themselves," Prien told German public broadcaster ZDF on Thursday. In addition to requesting age checks, Prien said media education and providing more information on the issue to parents are key. On Wednesday, the president of the European Commission , Ursula von der Leyen , proposed that children under the age of 13 be banned from accessing social media platforms such as TikTok , Snapchat, and Instagram. They would be able to use "mini-accounts" controlled and supervised by parents, with a maximum usage of one hour per day, and open a separate account from the age of 15. Changes to social media platforms Prien said the restrictions should be part of a broader, more comprehensive strategy. She also called for a rule under which children under the age of three have no screen time or access to digital services. The education minister announced plans as early as October for a German interim solution while rules are consolidated at the EU level. Under the EU proposals, social media platforms would be required to introduce safer designs, including measures to prevent endless scrolling and videos from playing automatically. Read the full story here . https://p.dw.com/p/5Ml95 Skip next section Authorities advice mosquito protection amid Malaria cases near Frankfurt Airport 09/17/2026 September 17, 2026 Authorities advice mosquito protection amid Malaria cases near Frankfurt Airport Frankfurt Aiport is Germany's main international travel hub Image: Andreas Beil/IMAGO Health authorities in Frankfurt are advising residents to consider taking precautions against mosquitoes after several recent malaria cases in the region believed to have been caused by the insects having stowed away on aircraft. This week, two people living in the vicinity of Frankfurt Airport were reported to have contracted malaria. In August, two Frankfurt Airport employees died after contracting malaria in an outbreak believed to have been caused by infected mosquitoes brought into Germany on an aircraft. Four other workers were infected, but recovered without complications. The cases are part of a rare outbreak of so-called airport malaria, with the six employees infected despite not having traveled to a malaria-risk country. Authorities have not shared details about the two cases this week. According to Germany's Robert Koch health institute, cases of airport malaria are extremely rare. Data cited by DPA news agency shows that between 1969 and 2024, only 145 cases of locally contracted malaria were reported in Europe. At least 105 of those cases involved mosquitoes arriving on planes. Most of these cases were in France, with only 9 reported in Germany in this time frame, making the 2026 outbreak a statistical outlier. Malaria is native to tropical environments, and the vast majority of cases in Europe occur in summer. Police said explosives were set off shortly after 4 a.m. in front of a cafe in the city's "Nordend" neighborhood, and a few minutes later in front of a kiosk in the city center. No injuries were reported. Images of the cafe showed a shattered glass facade and shards blown out onto the street. "We have officers on the scene," a police spokeswoman told Germany's DPA news agency. "We're working hard on it," she added, referring to the ongoing investigation. Police have not released any information about a motive or possible suspects. In the past few days, there had been two explosions in Frankfurt and one in nearby Offenbach. The entrance to an apartment building in Frankfurt was damaged by a blast on Monday Image: Mike Seeboth/dpa/picture alliance Early Sunday morning, there were also explosions in Frankfurt's Sachsenhausen district and in Offenbach. A bar, a cafe, and a newsstand were damaged in the incidents. Following the explosion in Sachsenhausen, a 15-year-old suspect was arrested and is currently in pretrial detention. This week's blasts come after repeated explosions in the Rhine-Main region over the past weeks and months. Police have attributed several of these incidents to organized crime and the phenomenon of "violence as a service," in which teenagers and young adults are specifically recruited to carry out these acts, local public broadcaster HR reported. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/c62keq.text: An Australian bandâs âunrealâ journey to break a gig world record An Australian bandâs âunrealâ journey to break a gig world record Close Dream rock band Fathom travelled roughly 700km across Australia to play nine shows, setting a new Guinness World Record for most concerts performed in 12 hours across multiple cities. In order to beat the record, venues needed to be at least 50km apart in cities populated by more than 15,000 people, with half of the cities needing to have populations of at least 100,000. Fathom partnered with a mental health service, Beyond Blue, donating half of the revenue from ticket sales and merchandise. The BBC sat down with the duo to recount the day full of excitement and hurdles. Photograph: EPA View image in fullscreen People evacuated from the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky arrive in Ukraine at an undisclosed location. Photograph: EPA Ukraine Oleshky evacuees reunite with families after truce allows crossing back into Ukraine Residents of nearby villages line highway waving flags to greet the evacuees’ convoy from the Russian-occupied city Associated Press Sat 31 Oct 2026 15.17 EDT Last modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 15.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky have been reunited with their families after crossing into Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday. The major rescue operation began on Friday and was carried out under the most significant truce since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago. Evacuees wrapped in Ukrainian flags stepped off buses at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border to be reunited with family members. Volunteers with hand-drawn welcome signs handed coffee to the weary people who had travelled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus. Residents of nearby villages lined the highway waving flags and torches to greet the convoy. Evacuation of civilians begins in besieged Ukrainian city of Oleshky Read more Tetiana Leonidivna, 71, thanked the Ukrainian soldiers who helped her to flee. “We love them, we love them,” she said through tears. “We know that they are protecting us. And a deep bow to them, and a deep bow to their parents, for having such children. I am proud, I am simply proud.” The ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region began early on Tuesday and was expected to continue through Sunday evening. The White House said the first lady Melania Trump helped broker the localised deal, while Pope Leo XIV pressed Russia and Ukraine to allow aid deliveries and evacuations. Relatives and volunteers with the Red Cross, Médecins Sans Frontières and World Central Kitchen welcomed the evacuees as they arrived at the border, ready to provide aid and food, including for their pets. View image in fullscreen Dmytro and Larysa were delighted to return to Ukrainian-controlled territory. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters Holding a cigarette between shaking fingers, 48-year-old Ivan Yevhenovych described his last months in Oleshky. “It was very difficult. There were a lot of drones. It was hard to move around the streets,” he said. “Since spring, there hasn’t really been any staple food left. People had a little bit of their own reserves. We are thrifty people.” He said landmines or drone strikes were killing residents every day. An estimated 2,000 people remained in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold. They were offered the choice of being evacuated to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies. “Many people stayed behind and didn’t want to leave,” Yevhenovych said. “Some for their houses, some for their animals.” View image in fullscreen Relatives and volunteers welcomed the evacuees at the border, ready to provide aid and food, including for their pets. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters Ukrainian authorities, seeking to protect those who remained and safeguard future humanitarian missions, have not said how many residents evacuated Oleshky and have restricted details of their route. Melania Trump posted on social media on Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people. Liza Paliy, 19, waited at the border for her father, whom she last saw more than two and a half years earlier when she fled the occupied city with her mother and sister. “We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately two years have already passed,” she said. Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, hailed the humanitarian mission as a win. “This is an extremely important moment. Behind us are difficult negotiations, agreements, preparations, and an enormous amount of work. But most importantly, the people who waited so long to be rescued are finally safe,” he said in an online post. Lubinets said evacuees ranged in age from just over one year old to 94, and they brought pets, including dogs, cats, a parrot and a raccoon. He said he hoped the Oleshky truce could be replicated elsewhere, saying it “could form the basis of a new mechanism for responding to the most difficult humanitarian crises”. View image in fullscreen Evacuees ranged in age from just over one year old to 94. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters Yana Lantratova, Russia’s human rights commissioner, said both sides have agreed to conduct regular humanitarian missions in and around Oleshky. Lubinets did not mention this development. “The mission has concluded, but, unfortunately, living conditions in Oleshky remain extremely difficult,” she said. “We will make every effort to support those residents who have made the decision to stay.” Some Oleshky evacuees who chose to move to Russian-occupied territory were taken to a temporary shelter in Simferopol, Lantratova said. The city is in Ukraine’s Crimean peninsula, which Moscow annexed in 2014. “After everything they have endured and a long journey, it is essential for these people to rest, recover and feel cared for. However, support should not be limited to just a roof over their heads and a hot meal,” she said in a social media post.
